item.title: If you are a product leader, here is a simple exercise: draw out your product lifecycle. e.g. market understanding -> design -> development -> GTM. Chances are your PMs spend more time in some stages than others - because of the nature of your product, your org or their comfort zones. This is a h...
item.description:
作者：Madhu Guru 账号：@realmadhuguru 简介：Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.
If you are a product leader, here is a simple exercise: draw out your product lifecycle.
e.g. market understanding -> design -> development -> GTM.
Chances are your PMs spend more time in some stages than others - because of the nature of your product, your org or their comfort zones.
This is a handoff-heavy, lossy process.
Now ask yourself: using AI, how much deeper can PMs go on every stage?
PMs should be able to - build a much deeper, broader understanding of users and the market - iterate fast from ideas to working prototypes - explore the codebase to study technical constraints and tradeoffs - run their own analytics and investigate questions as they emerge - understand the GTM funnel deeply enough to shape product strategy
Now, this is not about PMs replacing every role. As the function that spans the entire lifecycle, this is about raising the bar on the PM role, so they combine their breadth with much greater depth.

item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
So bullish on MCP. Its utility exceeds the "M" part: even AI aside, it'll be a civilization-scale accomplishment to get all our systems communicating through one universal open protocol.
A missing piece was how to get arbitrary callbacks across sessions. MCP could read and write, but it couldn't tell you later "this event happened." MCP Events fixes this.
We're adding support in our own MCP. Say an agent makes a deployment, and wants to know when it's complete. Instead of polling, it can subscribe to 𝚍𝚎𝚙𝚕𝚘𝚢𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝.𝚜𝚞𝚌𝚌𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚎𝚍.
PSA: With Vercel Queues and Workflows, writing the backend machinery for your own MCPs to do this is easy peasy.

item.description:
作者：Dan Shipper 账号：@danshipper 简介：ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI
BREAKING:
@AnthropicAI just dropped Claude Fable 5.2. It’s a paradigm-shifting model if you have a project ambitious enough to give it.
We’ve been testing it at @every, and I’ve seen this crazy explosion of creativity on the team. People are making their own creative software, games for their kids, and documentaries instead of slide decks.
Here’s your day zero vibe check:
• Coding: @kieranklaassen built Everycut, a video editor with the features we use from Premiere, Descript, and other tools—all in one app, with an agent built in. The first version was live in 3 days, and we immediately used it for our internal show-and-tell. This feels like a new era of professionals building their own professional tools, tailored to exactly how they work.
• Games and design: @jackcheng gave it a photo of his toddler’s messy playroom. It turned the actual toys into a playable racing game, with fun details like a stray shoe as an obstacle and a sippy cup as a power-up.
• Knowledge work: @hammer_mt turned his research into a documentary. The model came up with interview questions, he answered them on camera, and it cut the footage together. He called this the most productive 3 weeks of his career.
• A different way of working: Give it a big job and leave it running overnight or over a weekend. But tell it what “done” means: Mike found it could finish the build, then spend another day or two testing. Set the goal, the budget, and how much checking you need before walking away.
• The catch: It’s slow and burns through tokens. Our early-access usage was free, and these projects would have been expensive at API rates. It’s 20% cheaper than Fable 5.1, but for everyday writing, emails, or quick back-and-forth coding, I’d usually reach for something else.
The clearest signal: When our early access ended, @TylerNishida stopped working on some projects until he could get this model back. He didn’t want to build them with anything else.
The best measure of a new model is whether it makes you try things you wouldn’t have tried before.
Fable 5.2 absolutely does that.

Um, so, uh, you've done a bunch of podcasts, Garrett, especially you [chuckles] on, on, uh, the transition from Handshake to Handshake AI, uh, and just introducing that, their overall business, so we're not gonna go, go into that.
I'll recommend Lenny, who is a friend of the pod, uh, who did an excellent podcast with you guys. Um, so I, I think, like, what we're trying to really nail today is the s- state of data, the frontier of data.
Um, to me, I care a lot about data quality. This is what I base, uh, my whole track on AIE for. Um, and we also are interested in, I guess, the buying process and how, how the state of data has kind of moved, right?
Like, before recording, you guys have said, uh, or at least, um, n- sh- uh, you, you, you're saying that, um,
labeling has moved from, like, let's, let's call it, like, the, the average college student at, like, ten dollars an hour, which is what I used to do in my college years- Mm-hmm... to, like, professors.
Um, I don't know if you guys wanna comment on, on that. Yeah. Um, I mean, there's, like, a, a bunch of different dimensions that, like, this industry has, like, evolved in.
If you rewind, you know, certainly there was, like, true data labeling, which is drawing- you know, I think the image people have in their head is, like, drawing boxes around cars or, you know, sentiment, uh, categorization of, of a social media post or something like that.
Um, and there's still some of that around to, to some extent, right, as it gets more nuanced and, and language evolves.
But, um, you know, uh, uh, when language models first came onto the scene, you know, late 2022 or early 2023, we did a bunch of RLHF and-- But the models were kind of putting out gibberish, right?
And so you could still have, like, a high school student or a college student, um, very easily just sort of train these models en masse, right?
Um, but over the last, like, three years, uh, they've gotten pretty good, at least seemingly, at producing language and complex thought.
We've trained them how to reason through problems, how to call tools, how to, you know, do a lot more complex things.
Um, and so now, uh, we're, we're certainly at a point where, uh, you typically need some level of real expertise to be able to train these models, um, you know, whether that's, you know, being an investment banker or that's being a lawyer or a doctor, whatever it is.
Um, I do think there's, like, a little bit of a misconception that, like, that only increases, right?
Like, we're still seeing, like, two-year investment bankers who are more than capable of training these models in a lot of depth.
Um, so I don't, you know, necessarily think that you need a, the best professor in the world to train models right now.
Like, certainly there's things where you wanna train them at that frontier of, of, of knowledge, but still, there's a lot of things that models fail on, which I know we'll, we'll get to later, in just, like, you know, a typical one-year investment banker job, right?
Um, but I think that the core change has been, like, what is the task? These people aren't, like, drawing boxes around cars.

Like, we're building these really complex, you know, simulated worlds, these RL environments where, you know, someone basically needs to author a world, you know, that is reflective of what an agent would have to do in, in production in a bank, in a law firm, in a, in a hospital, whatever it is.
Um, that world that you're authoring has to be realistic. It has to be complex, reflective of all the nuance and mess that the real world has.
Um, and then on top of that, you've gotta write your, you know, whatever task that you want the agent to do, and what's much harder is then defining what good looks like, right?

Humans are not great and have not really had the muscle of, like, really explaining and codifying what good looks like consistently for longer and longer and longer time length or horizon tasks.
And so the shape of data and, like, what these people have to do, what these experts have to do is just so on the polar end, opposite end of, of what data labeling was, um, that I just think the verb is, like, totally incorrect- Yeah...
at this point, right? It's just experts now, not- It's experts, like, authoring data. Yeah. I mean, I guess walk us through it, right? Are they creating rubrics?

What, what goes into it? Yeah, it's, I mean, it's all the above.

So for example, um, let's, let's give a concrete example. I wanna build, uh, a unit of data for, uh, an investment banking task that I'll have in an eval, and, and we'll get into way more details on that.
